sections.normalized_html:
Recall that two graphs [MATH: G=(V_G,E_G)] and [MATH: H=(V_H,E_H)] are isomorphic if there exists a bijection [MATH: f : V_G \to V_H] such that [MATH: (u,v) \in E_G \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad (f(u),f(v)) \in E_H.]

If two graphs are isomorphic, their properties, e.g., the degrees of the vertices, cycles, connectivity, etc., are identical.

Let's write down the degrees of the vertices of each tree (in ascending order):

  • The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_1] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 2]

  • The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_2] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 3]

  • The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_3] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 4]

  • The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_4] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 3]

Only [MATH: G_2] and [MATH: G_4] have the same collection of degrees. So, they are the only two that could be isomorphic. However, notice that the vertices of degree [MATH: 2] are not adjacent in [MATH: G_2] (see below on the left).

On the other hand, the vertices of degree [MATH: 2] are adjacent in [MATH: G_4] (see above on the right). Thus, [MATH: G_2] and [MATH: G_4] are not isomorphic.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the trees are isomorphic to each other."

A rooted tree is a tree with one vertex designated as the root. When drawing a rooted tree, we usually place the root at the top and arrange the other vertices below by levels: the [MATH: 1]st level contains vertices that are at a distance [MATH: 1] from the root in the original tree, the [MATH: 2]nd level, those at a distance [MATH: 2], and so on.

Content:
This result follows from Cayley's formula for the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices, [MATH: |T_n| = n^{n-2}.] Since each labeled tree can be rooted at any of its [MATH: n] vertices, we apply the Product Rule:
[MATH: |T_{n}^{′}||= (# of choices for the root) × (# of labeled trees); = n ⋅ n^{n − 2}; = n^{n − 1}.]

[MATH: |T_{3}^{′}||= 3^{3 − 1}; = 3^{2}; = 9.]

items.title: Counting the Number of Labeled Rooted Trees

sections.normalized_html: How many labeled rooted trees are there on [MATH: 17] vertices?
sections.readable_text: How many labeled rooted trees are there on [MATH: 17] vertices?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A rooted tree is a tree in which one vertex has been designated the root.

Cayley's formula for the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices is [MATH: |T_n| = n^{n-2}.]

First, note that on [MATH: n] vertices, there are [MATH: n] choices for a tree's root. Then, by the rule of product, we have [MATH: # of labeled rooted trees|= (# of choices for the root) × (# of labeled trees); = n ⋅ n^{n − 2}; = n^{n − 1}.]

Therefore, the number of labeled rooted trees on [MATH: 17] vertices is [MATH: 17 ⋅|T_{17}||= 17 ⋅ 17^{17 − 2}; = 17^{17 − 1}; = 17^{16}.]

Content:
Cayley's formula for counting the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices is given by
[MATH: T(n) = n^{n-2}.]

Content:
There are multiple ways to prove this theorem. Here, we'll use a so-called double counting method. We will count the number of labeled out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices using two separate methods and equate them, which yields an explicit formula for [MATH: T(n).]

Content:
Method 1 - Rooting and Edge Labeling:

Content:
Suppose we have a tree on [MATH: n] labeled vertices, like the tree shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4d78ee4960d2e0831597f8eca915956b]

Content:
We select one of the vertices as the root vertex.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/65bc1db968ec7f51fe95e513ac5ce1ea]

Content:
Our selection of the root vertex induces a natural direction of the edges "away" from the root vertex. This type of structure is called an out-tree and is unique for a given tree and choice of root.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6d466058caaa583c6d0a26367d6a414f]

Content:
Since there are [MATH: n] vertices in our tree, we have [MATH: (n-1)] edges. Suppose we assign labels [MATH: e_1, e_2, \ldots e_{n-1}] to these edges. One such configuration is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dc1ce2d99810f4154f21e0952c0a7ef1]

Content:
We call this configuration a sequenced out-tree. Since there are [MATH: (n-1)] edges, we have [MATH: (n-1)!] ways of assigning our edge labels.

Content:
For a given tree, we have a choice of [MATH: n] vertices as the root and [MATH: (n-1)!] ways of assigning the edge labels. Therefore, the total number of sequenced out-trees for a given tree is
[MATH: \textrm{# sequenced out-trees for a given tree} = n\cdot (n-1)! = n!]
and since there are [MATH: T(n)] possible labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices, the total number of sequenced out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices equals
[MATH: n]

Content:
Method 2 – Sequential Construction:

Content:
We now count the number of sequenced out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices using a different method.

Content:
Suppose we initiate a rooted forest on [MATH: n] vertices with no edges. Each vertex is a rooted tree, and our forest has [MATH: n] rooted trees.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5b6174e0bad13c85f244e64a7626c09d]

Content:
[MATH: e_1,]

Content:
[MATH: e_2,]

Content:
[MATH: e_3,]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b6b2beb26d99f3a4481a05012c0b2435]

Content:
Suppose we have already added [MATH: n-k] edges to our tree, which means our forest currently contains [MATH: k] rooted trees.

Content:
To assign the next edge, we must choose a starting vertex (the tail of our directed edge) and an end vertex (the head of our directed edge):

Content:
- For the starting vertex, we can choose any of the [MATH: n] vertices on the graph.
- To end with a sequenced out-tree, we cannot select any vertex in the graph as the end vertex. Instead, we must choose a root vertex in another rooted tree of our forest. In other words, it must be a root vertex, but it cannot be the root vertex in the same tree as our starting vertex. Once selected, the end vertex is no longer a root vertex.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c15ff6170351205f85c10d455618572d]

Content:
- Since our graph contains [MATH: k] rooted trees, we have [MATH: (k-1)] choices of edge for a given vertex.
- Therefore, the number of choices available for the next edge equals [MATH: n(k-1).]

Content:
Now, we have [MATH: n(k-1)] choices at every step. Therefore, the total number of directed out-trees equals

Content:
[MATH: # sequenced out-trees on n vertices|= n(n − 1) ⋅ n(n − 2) ⋅ n(n − 3)⋯n ⋅ 1; = n^{n − 1} ⋅ (n − 1)!; = n^{n − 2} ⋅ n!]

Content:
Equating the results from both methods, we have
[MATH: n!\cdot T(n) = n^{n-2} n!]
which finally yields Cayley's formula
[MATH: T(n) = n^{n-2}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that two graphs [MATH: G=(V_G,E_G)] and [MATH: H=(V_H,E_H)] are isomorphic if there exists a bijection [MATH: f : V_G \to V_H] such that
[MATH: (u,v) \in E_G
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
\left(f(u),f(v)\right) \in E_H.]

Content:
Put plainly, [MATH: G] and [MATH: H] are isomorphic if relabeling the vertices and edges of [MATH: H] gives the same graph as [MATH: G.]

Content:
Two isomorphic graphs share all structural properties, including vertex degrees, cycles, connectivity, and others.
The isomorphism of trees is defined in the same way as for all graphs.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Isomorphic Trees

Example Prompt:

Which of the trees above are isomorphic?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that two graphs [MATH: G=(V_G,E_G)] and [MATH: H=(V_H,E_H)] are isomorphic if there exists a bijection [MATH: f : V_G \to V_H] such that
[MATH: (u,v) \in E_G
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
(f(u),f(v)) \in E_H.]

If two graphs are isomorphic, their properties, e.g., the degrees of the vertices, cycles, connectivity, etc., are identical.

Let's write down the degrees of the vertices of each tree (in ascending order):

- The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_1] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 2]
- The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_2] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 3]
- The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_3] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 4]
- The degrees of the vertices in [MATH: G_4] are the following: [MATH: 1, \quad 1, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 2, \quad 3]

Only [MATH: G_2] and [MATH: G_4] have the same collection of degrees. So, they are the only two that could be isomorphic. However, notice that the vertices of degree [MATH: 2] are not adjacent in [MATH: G_2] (see below on the left).

[IMG: /graphics/f61b53d32423653f02d1657d41e9730c]

On the other hand, the vertices of degree [MATH: 2] are adjacent in [MATH: G_4] (see above on the right). Thus, [MATH: G_2] and [MATH: G_4] are not isomorphic.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the trees are isomorphic to each other."

An unlabeled graph is a graph in which vertices are indistinguishable, and only the structure (connections) matter. In this case, all isomorphic graphs are considered the same, regardless of their labeling.

Item 10 — Tutorial: Using Cayley's Formula on Rooted Trees

Content:
A rooted tree is a tree with one vertex designated as the root. When drawing a rooted tree, we usually place the root at the top and arrange the other vertices below by levels: the [MATH: 1]st level contains vertices that are at a distance [MATH: 1] from the root in the original tree, the [MATH: 2]nd level, those at a distance [MATH: 2], and so on.

Content:
For example, consider the tree shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7435f7b4bc8cfb965431c0f532e30d9a]

Content:
Suppose we designate the vertex [MATH: v_{10}] as the root. In this case, we may redraw the rooted tree by levels as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6a4e7049c389247ee9582f8ec7ffd2fb]

Content:
The number of labeled rooted trees on [MATH: n] vertices is
[MATH: |T'_n| = n^{n-1}.]

Content:
This result follows from Cayley's formula for the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices, [MATH: |T_n| = n^{n-2}.] Since each labeled tree can be rooted at any of its [MATH: n] vertices, we apply the Product Rule:
[MATH: |T_{n}^{′}||= (# of choices for the root) × (# of labeled trees); = n ⋅ n^{n − 2}; = n^{n − 1}.]

Content:
For example, the number of labeled rooted trees on [MATH: 3] vertices is
[MATH: |T_{3}^{′}||= 3^{3 − 1}; = 3^{2}; = 9.]

Item 11 — Example: Counting the Number of Labeled Rooted Trees

Example Prompt:
How many labeled rooted trees are there on [MATH: 17] vertices?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A rooted tree is a tree in which one vertex has been designated the root.

Cayley's formula for the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices is
[MATH: |T_n| = n^{n-2}.]

First, note that on [MATH: n] vertices, there are [MATH: n] choices for a tree's root. Then, by the rule of product, we have
[MATH: # of labeled rooted trees|= (# of choices for the root) × (# of labeled trees); = n ⋅ n^{n − 2}; = n^{n − 1}.]

Therefore, the number of labeled rooted trees on [MATH: 17] vertices is
[MATH: 17 ⋅|T_{17}||= 17 ⋅ 17^{17 − 2}; = 17^{17 − 1}; = 17^{16}.]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Using Cayley's Formula on Rooted Forests

Content:
A rooted forest is a graph in which each connected component is a rooted tree.

Content:
The number of labeled rooted forests on [MATH: n] vertices is
[MATH: |F_n| = (n+1)^{n-1}.]

Content:
This result follows from the bijection between the set [MATH: F_n] of all labeled rooted forests on [MATH: n] vertices and the set [MATH: T_{n+1}] of all labeled trees on [MATH: n+1] vertices. Since these sets are in one-to-one correspondence, they have the same cardinality:
[MATH: |F_{n}||=|T_{n + 1}|; = (n + 1)^{(n + 1) − 2}; = (n + 1)^{n − 1}]

Content:
For example, the number of labeled rooted forests on [MATH: 3] vertices is
[MATH: |F_{3}||= (3 + 1)^{3 − 1}; = 4^{2}; = 16.]

A rooted tree is a tree in which one vertex has been designated the root.
A rooted forest is a graph in which each connected component is a rooted tree.

Cayley's formula for the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices is
[MATH: |T_n| = n^{n-2}.]

First, note that there is a bijection between the set [MATH: F_n] of all labeled rooted forests on [MATH: n] vertices and the set [MATH: T_{n+1}] of all labeled trees on [MATH: n+1] vertices. As a result, these sets have the same cardinality:
[MATH: |F_{n}||=|T_{n + 1}|; = (n + 1)^{(n + 1) − 2}; = (n + 1)^{n − 1}]

Therefore, the number of labeled rooted forests on [MATH: 9] vertices is

[MATH: |F_{9}||= (9 + 1)^{9 − 1}; = 10^{8}.]

Item 18 — Tutorial: Proof of Cayley's Formula

Content:
Cayley's formula for counting the number of labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices is given by
[MATH: T(n) = n^{n-2}.]

Content:
There are multiple ways to prove this theorem. Here, we'll use a so-called double counting method. We will count the number of labeled out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices using two separate methods and equate them, which yields an explicit formula for [MATH: T(n).]

Content:
Method 1 - Rooting and Edge Labeling:

Content:
Suppose we have a tree on [MATH: n] labeled vertices, like the tree shown below.

Content:
Our selection of the root vertex induces a natural direction of the edges "away" from the root vertex. This type of structure is called an out-tree and is unique for a given tree and choice of root.

Graphic:

Content:
Since there are [MATH: n] vertices in our tree, we have [MATH: (n-1)] edges. Suppose we assign labels [MATH: e_1, e_2, \ldots e_{n-1}] to these edges. One such configuration is shown below.

Graphic:

Content:
We call this configuration a sequenced out-tree. Since there are [MATH: (n-1)] edges, we have [MATH: (n-1)!] ways of assigning our edge labels.

Content:
For a given tree, we have a choice of [MATH: n] vertices as the root and [MATH: (n-1)!] ways of assigning the edge labels. Therefore, the total number of sequenced out-trees for a given tree is
[MATH: \textrm{# sequenced out-trees for a given tree} = n\cdot (n-1)! = n!]
and since there are [MATH: T(n)] possible labeled trees on [MATH: n] vertices, the total number of sequenced out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices equals
[MATH: n]

Method 2 – Sequential Construction:

Content:
We now count the number of sequenced out-trees on [MATH: n] vertices using a different method.

Content:
Suppose we initiate a rooted forest on [MATH: n] vertices with no edges. Each vertex is a rooted tree, and our forest has [MATH: n] rooted trees.

Content:
Suppose we have already added [MATH: n-k] edges to our tree, which means our forest currently contains [MATH: k] rooted trees.

Content:
To assign the next edge, we must choose a starting vertex (the tail of our directed edge) and an end vertex (the head of our directed edge):

Content:
- For the starting vertex, we can choose any of the [MATH: n] vertices on the graph.
- To end with a sequenced out-tree, we cannot select any vertex in the graph as the end vertex. Instead, we must choose a root vertex in another rooted tree of our forest. In other words, it must be a root vertex, but it cannot be the root vertex in the same tree as our starting vertex. Once selected, the end vertex is no longer a root vertex.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c15ff6170351205f85c10d455618572d]

Content:
- Since our graph contains [MATH: k] rooted trees, we have [MATH: (k-1)] choices of edge for a given vertex.
- Therefore, the number of choices available for the next edge equals [MATH: n(k-1).]

Content:
Now, we have [MATH: n(k-1)] choices at every step. Therefore, the total number of directed out-trees equals

Content:
[MATH: # sequenced out-trees on n vertices|= n(n − 1) ⋅ n(n − 2) ⋅ n(n − 3)⋯n ⋅ 1; = n^{n − 1} ⋅ (n − 1)!; = n^{n − 2} ⋅ n!]

Content:
Equating the results from both methods, we have
[MATH: n!\cdot T(n) = n^{n-2} n!]
which finally yields Cayley's formula
[MATH: T(n) = n^{n-2}.]
